o: Flag users having two purchases whose dates are within 7 days of each other (inclusive window). The table may contain duplicate records, so we must compare distinct purchase events and avoid pairing a row with itself. User 6 in the example qualifies (Sep 10 → Sep 14 is 4 days); user 4 does not (11 days apart).
k: Self-join per user with DATEDIFF in [0, 7], excluding trivial self-pairs.
DISTINCT collapses duplicate rows before/after matching.
Alternatively LAG over per-user chronological purchases after de-duplication.

a.i: Join the Users table to itself on user_id where the second purchase falls 0–7 days after the first. Guard against a row pairing with itself by requiring the (date, item) pairs differ; DISTINCT then yields each qualifying user once.
s: Self-join Users U1, U2 on user_id.
Require 0 ≤ DATEDIFF(U2.created_at, U1.created_at) ≤ 7 and the records not identical.

c.python:
-- MySQL (Database problem; SQL shown for all language slots)
SELECT DISTINCT U1.user_id
FROM Users U1
JOIN Users U2
  ON U1.user_id = U2.user_id
 AND U1.created_at <= U2.created_at
 AND DATEDIFF(U2.created_at, U1.created_at) <= 7
 AND (U1.created_at <> U2.created_at OR U1.item <> U2.item);

a.t: O(N²) pairwise comparisons in the worst case (index on user_id helps)

a.i: De-duplicate rows in a CTE, then use LAG to fetch each purchase's previous date for the same user; a gap ≤ 7 days marks the user active. This scans data once per partition and scales better than the join.
s: CTE with SELECT DISTINCT user_id, item, created_at.
LAG(created_at) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY created_at) as prev.
Filter DATEDIFF(created_at, prev) <= 7; select DISTINCT user_id.
a.t: O(N log N) per-partition sort for the window

w: The LAG solution is cleaner and faster; the self-join works on older MySQL. Pitfalls: NULL gap from LAG (filtered automatically by the comparison), duplicate rows creating phantom pairs, and the inclusivity of the 7-day window. Follow-up: active in every rolling week, or top-K most active users.
